chunks: Hammad narrated from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a man whom a woman appointed as her agent in her marriage affairs, whether she is a relative or a neighbor of his, and he does not know the hidden details of her case; if he found that she had concealed a defect in herself, he said: 'The dowry is taken from her, and there is no liability on the one who married her.'

And he said regarding a woman who appointed a man as her agent, and she said to him: 'Marry me to so-and-so.' He said: 'I will not marry you until you testify that my affair is in your hand.' So she testified to him. Then he said at the time of marriage to the one proposing to her: 'O so-and-so, upon you is such and such.' He said: 'Yes.' Then he said to the people: 'Bear witness that that is for her with me, and I have married her to myself.' The woman said: 'I did not marry you except out of courtesy, and my affair is not in your hand, and I did not appoint you as my agent except out of shyness from speaking.'
He said: 'He is removed from her, and his head is struck (or he is punished).'.

key_terms.دَخِيلَةُ الْأَمْرِ: Hidden details or inner state of the case
key_terms.وَكِيل: Agent or representative in legal affairs

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a marriage agent if the woman conceals a defect or uses the agency merely as a formality?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the mechanics of *wakalah* (agency) in marriage, distinguishing between genuine delegation and mere formality. In the first case, if the agent is unaware of hidden defects, he bears no liability, emphasizing the importance of transparency in contractual agency. In the second, where the woman retains actual control but uses the agent out of modesty (*hayā’*), the agent is penalized for acting as a mere conduit rather than a true representative, highlighting the Shia juristic focus on the intent and actual authority behind legal acts.
